title: What is Space-Based architecture (in-memory data grid to remove the DB bottleneck), and when is it justified (extreme bursty load: trading, ticketing)?
shortTitle: What is Space-Based architecture, and when is it justified?
keyPoints: Space-Based architecture keeps hot data in a replicated in-memory grid so requests hit memory instead of a database.
Each processing unit holds business logic and a slice of the data, serving reads and writes from RAM.
A separate data-writer process flushes changes to the backing database asynchronously, off the critical path.
Scaling works by adding processing units, each bringing its own memory and CPU, giving roughly linear throughput growth.
It is justified only when the database is the proven bottleneck under extreme bursty load such as trading, flash sales, or ticketing.
Trade-offs include eventual consistency between the grid and the database, durability risk if replicas fail before a flush, and high operational complexity.
Simpler options like caching, read replicas, and sharding should be exhausted before reaching for this architecture.

s1_definition.oneliner: Put the hot data in a replicated in-memory grid so requests hit memory instead of a database, scale by adding grid nodes, and flush to the database asynchronously – use it only when the database truly cannot keep up with extreme bursty load.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Processing Unit** – an application instance that contains both the business logic and an in-memory data grid holding the data it needs, so reads and writes hit RAM with no database round trip.
- **In-Memory Data Grid** – a distributed, partitioned, replicated store (Hazelcast, Apache Ignite, Coherence) that spans all processing units and keeps data consistent across them.
- **Data Writer (Data Pump)** – a separate asynchronous process that reads changes from the grid and persists them to a backing database, taking the database off the critical path.
- **Messaging Grid** – distributes incoming requests across processing units so each handles a share of the load.
- **Scaling Model** – capacity grows by adding processing units, each bringing its own memory and CPU, giving roughly linear throughput growth with no single database to scale.
s1_definition.analogy: On a normal day at National Bank of India the single ledger clerk at the back (the central database) can handle every request. But on market-open morning, thousands of trade orders arrive in seconds, and that one clerk becomes a hopeless bottleneck. Space-Based architecture is like giving every counter its own fast in-memory notepad holding the data it needs, so counters serve customers instantly without waiting for the back clerk. The notepads sync with each other so they agree, and a separate quiet clerk copies everything from the notepads into the permanent ledger in the background, off the critical path.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Space-Based architecture exists to remove the central database as the bottleneck under extreme load. The insight is that you can add as many application servers as you like, but if they all funnel into one database, that database saturates on connections, locks, and disk I/O, and latency spikes no matter what. Space-Based architecture takes the database off the hot path by keeping application state in an in-memory data grid, replicated and partitioned across processing units, so reads and writes hit memory instead of disk.

The architecture has processing units that combine business logic with an in-memory slice of the data, an in-memory data grid like Hazelcast or Apache Ignite that is distributed across those units, a messaging grid that spreads requests, and a separate data writer that asynchronously flushes changes from the grid to the backing database. Because you scale by adding processing units, each bringing its own memory and CPU, throughput grows roughly linearly and there is no single database to scale, which is exactly why it absorbs bursts.

The trade-offs are serious. Because writes are flushed asynchronously, there is a window where the database lags the grid, so if a unit and its replica both fail before the flush you can lose recent writes. The grid and database are eventually consistent, which is unacceptable for invariants that need the database as the instant source of truth. In-memory grids are operationally complex, and holding large datasets in RAM across many nodes is expensive. The mature judgment is to reach for this only after caching, read replicas, and sharding have failed to meet a genuinely extreme bursty load.

Remember one sentence: keep hot data in a replicated in-memory grid so requests hit memory instead of the database, scale by adding grid nodes, and flush to the database asynchronously, but reserve it for extreme bursty load because the cost and complexity are substantial.
